name: Glycolic acid peel

card.summary: The most widely studied AHA peel, tested in melasma, periorbital darkening and acne scars in mostly small studies.
card.note: Stinging, redness and dryness are common; home kits have been associated with injury.

quick.overview:
A glycolic acid peel exfoliates the skin using an alpha-hydroxy acid and is used for pigmentation, acne scars and general texture.

It has the largest body of small comparative studies among the common peels, though many are from single centers.
quick.mechanism: It is a mild superficial peel that loosens the outer skin layers, which then shed.
quick.risks: Common effects are stinging, redness, irritation and dryness; pigment change is among reported complications, and Wikipedia notes weak home kits can cause injury and scarring.

lead: A glycolic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel using glycolic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA). It is used to make skin look smoother, brighter and more even: Wikipedia describes AHA peels as the mildest peels, used for fine wrinkles, dryness, uneven pigment and acne, and one review calls glycolic acid the most common AHA peel, described by its author as simple, inexpensive and low in downtime [11][17].

The acid loosens the bonds between dead surface skin cells so the top layer sheds, revealing fresher skin and reducing visible pigment and texture irregularities. Professional peels use higher concentrations applied in an office, and lower-strength versions are sold for home use [11][12][13]. Studies in Indian and other patient groups have examined glycolic peels, at concentrations such as 20%, 30%, 35% or 70%, for melasma, periorbital melanosis and acne scars, alone, against other peels, or combined with microneedling and other treatments [1][2][3][4][8][18][19].

The peel's depth depends on acid concentration, the number of coats and contact time, so the same agent can be used as a very light or a medium-depth peel, with neutralisation at the end of the contact time [17]. Glycolic acid occurs naturally in sugarcane, sugar beets, pineapple, cantaloupe and unripe grapes, and was named by Auguste Laurent in 1848 [13].

chain: Glycolic acid applied to the face for a short period
Loosens and sheds the surface layer of dead skin cells
Smoother texture and more even tone, with fewer visible dark patches or mild scars
angle.text: People use glycolic peels, usually in a series spaced weeks apart, to brighten skin, soften fine texture and fade pigment such as melasma or post-acne marks. Results build over several sessions, and trials generally pair peels with sun protection or other topical treatments.

paras: Chemical peels remove the outermost skin layers by causing a controlled injury that makes the skin peel, usually on the face, and they are grouped by depth: light (AHA and BHA), medium (trichloroacetic acid) and deep (phenol-croton oil) [11]. Glycolic acid is the best-known AHA peel agent; salicylic acid is the beta-hydroxy counterpart, used for oilier, acne-prone skin [11]. Medium-depth peels are done by a medical provider, while light peels are the entry point [11]. Light peels usually need no anaesthetic, since patients feel only slight stinging [11]. Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Shilpi Khetarpal describes the sensation as mildly uncomfortable, with tingling, burning and heat [12].

Glycolic acid is a small molecule with a pKa of 3.83 that dissolves readily in water; it is also described as a keratolytic agent used in acne treatment [13]. Industrially it is made mainly by carbonylation of formaldehyde, and it can also be isolated from plant sources [13].

Chemical peeling has a long history. In the 19th century the Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra used agents such as phenol, croton oil and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities, phenol-croton oil peels were used quietly by early Hollywood stars in the 1920s, and they entered mainstream practice in the 1960s through Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon [11]. Light alpha-hydroxy acid peels are a more recent, gentler development of the same idea [11]. Glycolic acid itself was named by Auguste Laurent in 1848 and first prepared by Adolph Strecker and Nikolai Sokolov in 1851 [13].

AHAs moved into consumer skincare as exfoliating ingredients, with the FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review (CIR) expert panel reviewing their safety in the 1990s and 2000s [15][16]. The FDA received 114 adverse dermatologic reports for AHA skin-care products between 1992 and February 2004, peaking in 1994, with burning, rash, swelling and pigment change most frequent and the most serious reactions linked to the strongest exfoliating products, such as skin peelers [16].

Glycolic acid peels are among the agents studied for melasma, a pigment disorder with brown patches on the face, either alone or with topical lightening agents [2][5][9][17]. They have also been studied for periorbital melanosis, the dark circles around the eyes, and for acne-related pigmentation and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [1][3][17].

For acne scars, glycolic peels have been combined with microneedling in people with darker skin, where scars often coexist with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [1]. Light peels are also used for dryness and fine texture [11]. A review of glycolic acid peels covers acne, acne scars, melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, photoaging and seborrhea [17].
A Cochrane review of topical treatments for acne examined AHAs alongside azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur and zinc, including 49 randomised trials in all [22].

Glycolic acid is the smallest of the alpha hydroxy acids used in cosmetics, a family known for chemically exfoliating the skin; Wikipedia cites a 1994 supplement titled Alpha Hydroxy Acids for Skin Care and several peel and cream studies, including a 1999 report by Atzori and colleagues on glycolic peeling for acne and a 2001 study by Kalla and colleagues comparing glycolic and trichloroacetic acid peels for melasma [15].

Concentration and pH matter for how these products behave. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel considered glycolic and lactic acid safe for consumers when the AHA concentration is 10 percent or less, the final pH is 3.5 or higher, and the product either protects against increased sun sensitivity or directs daily sun protection [16]. This framework separates consumer products from the higher-strength peels given by providers [15][16]. The FDA notes that products sold for acne or skin lightening are considered drugs, and that skin peelers may contain high AHA concentrations [16].

Glycolic acid is described as a keratolytic agent, meaning it loosens and sheds the outer layer of skin, which is the basis for its use in peels for pigment, texture and acne [11][13]. Reviews describe peel depth as depending on concentration, number of coats and application time [17].

In professional settings, the review literature stresses patient history, skin examination and pre-peel skin priming, along with selecting patients and timing the neutralisation correctly [17]. Peels are generally given as a series separated by weeks, and trials combine them with sun protection or other topical treatments [2][19]. The review reports the peel as very safe in Fitzpatrick skin types I to IV, and does not address the darker types in its abstract [17]. Neutralisation can be done with a bicarbonate solution; a randomised split-face trial of 126 patients with skin phototypes IV and V examined water as the neutralising agent for a 35% peel [20].

Cleveland Clinic describes at-home peels as gentler than in-office peels, with a lower acid concentration that usually means several treatments before results appear. It lists AHAs (glycolic, lactic and mandelic acid) and the beta hydroxy acid salicylic acid as common ingredients, and advises patch testing and sun protection [12]. Home use in forum culture is mentioned in beginner skincare discussion; one 2003 T Nation poster describes a series of six weekly glycolic peels recommended by a facialist while treating breakouts [14].

Cleveland Clinic notes that people taking birth control pills, who are pregnant or who have a family history of discoloration have an increased risk of abnormal pigmentation after a peel, that prior retinoid use thins the outer skin so a peel may penetrate more deeply, and that people with a history of cold sores may have outbreaks [12]. The clinic advises avoiding tanning and sun exposure before a peel and using sunscreen afterwards [12].

The FDA cites a 2003 study conducted with its collaboration in which four weeks of topical AHA cream increased volunteers' sensitivity to UV-induced reddening by 18 percent and roughly doubled sensitivity to UV-induced cellular damage; the effect reversed within a week of stopping [16]. The agency recommends a sunburn alert on AHA products advising sun protection during use and for a week afterwards [16]. A National Toxicology Program study found glycolic acid did not affect photocarcinogenesis in mice [16].

Wikipedia notes that complications rise with peel depth and can include prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, skin thinning and photosensitivity, and that light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. It adds that both professional peels and low-strength home kits carry risks of injury and scarring [11]. Cleveland Clinic describes a sunburn-like reaction with redness, flaking and peeling lasting up to about a week or two depending on strength [12]. Glycolic acid in concentrated form is classed as corrosive and a skin irritant in chemical safety data [13].

In the periorbital melanosis comparison, adverse effects were most frequent with the glycolic peel, followed by the lactic peel and vitamin C [3]. In the melasma trial combining glycolic peels with azelaic acid, minor reversible side effects occurred in both groups and did not require stopping therapy [2]. In a trial of 35% glycolic peel alone for melasma, the glycolic-only group had the fewest side effects among the three arms [19].

A 2011 study combined microneedling with 35% glycolic acid peels for acne scars in dark skin: sixty patients were split between microneedling alone and microneedling with peels, and the combination group showed significant improvement in superficial and moderately deep scars, skin texture and post-acne pigmentation [1].

A 2017 randomised trial of sixty patients with atrophic acne scars compared microneedling alone with microneedling plus serial 70% glycolic acid peels [21]. A 2022 randomised trial of forty patients compared microneedling with a 35% glycolic peel against microneedling with a 15% trichloroacetic acid peel at two-week intervals; both combinations improved scar grades significantly with no significant difference between them, and more patients rated skin texture improvement as excellent or good in the glycolic group [18].

A 2017 study of sixty patients with epidermal melasma compared serial glycolic peels every three weeks plus 20% azelaic acid cream against the cream alone over 24 weeks; improvement in the melasma severity index was significantly greater in the peel group from week 12, with greater gains in melasma quality-of-life scores and only minor reversible side effects [2]. A 2019 trial of thirty melasma patients compared a 35% glycolic full-face peel alone with the same peel plus 10% or 20% trichloroacetic spot peels, four sessions fifteen days apart; all groups had significant reductions in the melasma area severity index with no significant difference between groups [19].

A comparative study of 90 patients with periorbital melanosis tested 20% glycolic peels, 15% lactic peels and 20% vitamin C over 12 weeks: more than 50% improvement occurred in about 73% of glycolic peel patients, 57% of lactic peel patients and 27% of vitamin C patients, and a later study added a 12% ferulic acid peel [3][4]. A 2024 randomised open-label study compared a 15% TCA peel with a 35% glycolic peel in acanthosis nigricans [23].

Registered trials include glycolic acid against salicylic acid for melasma [5][6], 70% glycolic acid with vitamin C for photoaging and acne scars [7][8], and a comparison against a 1064 nm Q-switched laser for melasma [9]. A 2025 systematic review of randomised trials covered topical treatments for acanthosis nigricans [10]. Many of the published studies are small and come from single centres.

Peels sit within a broader cosmetic-dermatology market for brightening and smoothing treatments, and appear in beginner skincare conversation on forums such as T Nation, where members discuss facial care routines [14]. Light peels are provided by dermatologists and licensed estheticians, and lower-strength versions are sold for home use [11][12].

lore.intro: Glycolic peels appear in skincare discussion as a first step beyond daily products for texture, marks and tone, and in discussion of home versus professional use [14][12].

claims.claim: Glycolic peels fade melasma and dark marks
claims.believers: Dermatology patients and practitioners using peels in series report lighter pigment, and trial reports describe the peel as a standard option [2][17].
claims.experts: Trials report significant reductions in melasma severity scores with glycolic peels, alone or with azelaic acid or TCA spot peels, in small studies [2][19].

claims.claim: Peels soften acne scars and texture
claims.believers: Skincare users pair peels with microneedling for scars and rough texture [1].
claims.experts: Randomised trials of microneedling with glycolic peels report improved scar grades and texture scores [1][18][21].

claims.claim: Glycolic peels clear acne and unclog pores
claims.believers: A 2003 T Nation poster describes breakouts improving after a series of weekly peels [14].
claims.experts: AHAs were examined in a Cochrane review of topical acne treatments, and trials of glycolic peels for acne exist [22][17].

claims.claim: Home peels give results similar to office peels
claims.believers: Consumer products are sold on this premise [12].
claims.experts: Cleveland Clinic says home peels are gentler with lower acid concentration and usually need several treatments, and the FDA and CIR set strength limits for consumer products [12][16].

claims.claim: Glycolic acid makes skin more sensitive to the sun
claims.believers: Brands and dermatologists advise strict sun protection during use [12].
claims.experts: A 2003 FDA-collaborating study found increased UV sensitivity during four weeks of AHA use that reversed within a week [16].

claims.believers: Some users move to higher-strength products for quicker change [12].
claims.experts: Reviews note depth depends on concentration, coats and time, and complications rise with depth; the FDA reports the most serious reactions with the strongest exfoliating products [11][16][17].
